tagline: The intersection with the most crashes in Michigan in 2025 is in Sterling Heights, where Van Dyke meets 18½ Mile and the M-53 freeway begins. Hall Road, Mound, and the mile roads carry the rest. At those intersections, fault is the case.

c.v: A car crash in Sterling Heights is a Michigan no-fault claim shaped by a few very busy roads. Van Dyke runs north through the city past the Stellantis plants and becomes the M-53 freeway at 18½ Mile. Hall Road (M-59) carries the retail traffic across the north. Mound carries the plant freight. Dequindre, Ryan, Schoenherr, Hayes, and the mile roads from Fourteen to Nineteen fill in the grid. In 2025, according to Michigan State Police crash data, 18½ Mile at Van Dyke recorded 210 crashes, more than any other intersection in Michigan; 11 Mile at Van Dyke in Warren was second. A Sterling Heights crash claim usually turns on two things: who had the right of way, and how much insurance is on the other side.

sections.heading: Where Sterling Heights crashes happen, and whose road it is

c.v: Van Dyke at 18½ Mile and the M-53 transition.

At 18½ Mile, Van Dyke, the M-53 freeway ramps, plant traffic, and retail traffic meet in one multilane roundabout. The crashes are failure-to-yield crashes at the entries, sideswipes and lane-change crashes inside the circle, rear-end crashes in the approach queues, and merge and weave crashes where the surface road becomes a freeway. South of there, Van Dyke runs past Sterling Heights Assembly and the supplier plants, with Metropolitan Parkway (16 Mile) fifth in Macomb County in 2025, with 77 crashes and 21 injuries.
Hall Road (M-59).

The retail corridor across the north of the city, from Dequindre to Hayes: big-box strips, restaurants, medical offices, and the former Lakeside Mall site, whose redevelopment will change traffic for years. Signal crashes at Van Dyke, Schoenherr, Hayes, and Mound; low-speed crashes and pedestrian strikes in the parking lots (see our
pedestrian accident page
); and the drivers leaving Hall Road’s restaurants and bars at night.
Mound Road.

The plant corridor, rebuilt from I-696 to M-59 in the Innovate Mound project, carrying tractor-trailers to and from Ford’s Sterling Axle Plant and the supplier plants at shift changes. Turning-truck crashes at the gates and rear-end crashes into slowing trucks are Mound’s cases; see our
Sterling Heights truck accident page
Dequindre and the Troy line.
Dequindre is the boundary with Oakland County, so a crash there can involve Troy drivers, Oakland County roads, and a choice of courts.
The mile roads and the subdivisions.

Fourteen through Nineteen Mile, Ryan, Schoenherr, Utica Road, and Hayes: signal crashes, and pedestrian and bicycle crashes near the schools, the parks along the Clinton River, and the subdivisions (see our
bicycle accident page
Three road agencies.

Van Dyke, Hall Road, and the M-53 freeway are MDOT’s; a road-defect claim against MDOT goes to the Court of Claims, with written notice filed there within 120 days (MCL 691.1404). The mile roads, Mound, Schoenherr, Ryan, Dequindre, and Hayes are generally the Macomb County Department of Roads’; subdivision streets are the City of Sterling Heights’; both take written notice within 120 days (MCL 691.1402, 691.1404). A pothole or other defect in the roadbed can make the agency a defendant alongside the other driver; on State and county roads, signals, signs, and sight obstructions generally fall outside the highway exception. Notice to the wrong agency is not notice.

In a rear-end crash, fault is rarely disputed. In a left-turn or signal crash at a Sterling Heights intersection, it is disputed often, and the other driver’s insurer may try to assign you half or more of the fault. That number matters: if you are found more than 50 percent at fault, you lose your claim for pain and suffering, and below that your recovery is reduced by your share (MCL 500.3135(2)(b)). At exactly 50 percent you recover half. The evidence that decides it is perishable:

sections.heading: Who pays after a Sterling Heights crash

c.v: Your no-fault (PIP) claim.

Your own auto insurer pays your medical expenses up to the PIP level you chose, 85 percent of lost wages for up to three years up to the monthly cap DIFS sets each October, replacement services at $20 a day, and attendant care, regardless of fault (MCL 500.3107). If you have no policy, a resident relative’s policy pays (MCL 500.3114); if none exists, the Michigan Assigned Claims Plan does (MCL 500.3172), capped at $250,000 for medical benefits. The insurer must receive written notice within one year (MCL 500.3145(1)) and must pay each bill within 30 days of reasonable proof or owe 12 percent interest (MCL 500.3142). Since the 2019 reform, PIP medical coverage is no longer unlimited unless you chose it, so the level on your declarations page matters. See our
no-fault insurance claim page
and
Michigan no-fault guide
Your claim against the at-fault driver.

For pain and suffering, you need a threshold injury: death, serious impairment of body function, or permanent serious disfigurement (MCL 500.3135(1)). A serious impairment is an objectively manifested impairment of an important body function that affects your general ability to lead your normal life; it does not have to be permanent (MCL 500.3135(5);
McCormick v Carrier

, 2010). You can also recover lost wages beyond the three years and medical bills above your chosen PIP level (MCL 500.3135(3)(c)). The suit must be filed within three years (MCL 600.5805(2)). The mini tort recovers up to $3,000 in vehicle damage not covered by your policy (MCL 500.3135(3)(e)), filed in the 41A District Court if the insurer will not pay it.
Coverage on the other side.
Many drivers carry the $50,000 minimum, and since 2019 many chose reduced PIP medical levels, which moves more of the bill into the claim against the at-fault driver. Your own
uninsured and underinsured motorist coverage

often decides what the claim is worth; we read every policy in the household before valuing the claim. Settling with the at-fault driver without your UIM insurer’s consent can forfeit the UIM claim. See our
uninsured motorist page
Drunk drivers and dram shop.

A crash caused by a drunk driver leaving a Hall Road restaurant or bar adds a claim against the business that served a visibly intoxicated person or a minor. Written notice must go to the retailer within 120 days after you hire a lawyer, the drunk driver must be named and kept in the suit, and the suit must be filed within two years, not three (MCL 436.1801(3), (4)). See our
drunk driving accident page
Government vehicles.

Sterling Heights Police and Fire, SMART buses on Van Dyke, Hall Road, and the mile roads, Utica Community Schools and Warren Consolidated Schools buses, and Department of Roads trucks fall under the motor vehicle exception to governmental immunity (MCL 691.1405). See our
bus accident page

faqs.question: Is 18½ Mile and Van Dyke really the most crash-prone intersection in Michigan?

answer.v: By count, yes, for 2025: Michigan State Police data recorded 210 crashes there, more than at any other intersection in the state. Second was 11 Mile at Van Dyke in Warren, with 180.

faqs.question: How many car accidents happen in Sterling Heights each year?

answer.v: Sterling Heights recorded 3,748 crashes, 1,119 injuries, and 8 deaths in 2024. Macomb County as a whole recorded 21,960 crashes, 6,596 injuries, and 70 deaths in 2024.

faqs.question: The other driver’s insurer says I was half at fault for a left turn on Van Dyke or Hall Road. Is my claim over?

answer.v: No. You lose the pain-and-suffering claim only if you are found more than 50 percent at fault. At 50 percent you recover half. The diagram, the signal data, the cameras, and the witnesses decide the number, not the adjuster.

faqs.question: I was hit by a driver leaving a Hall Road restaurant. Can I sue the restaurant?

answer.v: If it served a visibly intoxicated person who then caused the crash, yes, under the dram shop act, but notice must go out within 120 days after you hire a lawyer and the suit must be filed within two years.

faqs.question: The driver who hit me had no insurance. What now?

answer.v: Your no-fault benefits are unaffected: your own insurer, a household member’s, or the Assigned Claims Plan pays your medical bills and lost wages. Your pain-and-suffering claim depends on your uninsured motorist coverage.

faqs.question: Where would my Sterling Heights case be filed?

answer.v: Mini tort and claims up to $25,000 in the 41A District Court on Dodge Park Road; injury suits over $25,000 in the Sixteenth Judicial Circuit Court in Mount Clemens, or in some Dequindre cases the Oakland County Circuit Court.
One year to give your no-fault insurer written notice, three years to sue the at-fault driver, two years to sue a bar, and 120 days for a notice to the City or the Department of Roads.
